story.headline: Oil climbed back to about $110 overnight after the US ordered some diplomats and families out of Saudi Arabia following deadly Houthi attacks. Currencies barely moved; the Australian dollar hit a three-week high.

reads.policy: Almost every major central bank is leaning toward raising rates because high oil keeps inflation up. Hikes look near-certain soon in Britain, Canada and New Zealand, and likely by December in the US, the euro area and Japan. Switzerland is the odd one out, where a cut is still possible.
reads.growth: Growth is holding up but softening at the edges, with housing weak in the US and UK under high borrowing costs. That has not yet changed any central bank's plans, so it is not driving currencies for now.
reads.inflation: Inflation is running hot almost everywhere because of energy, which is why so many central banks are leaning toward hikes. New Zealand's figures overnight cooled slightly but stayed above target, so they did not change the picture. Japan's inflation figures tonight matter most for the yen.
reads.risk: The Gulf conflict moved closer to Saudi oil sites, and the US told some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia. Markets took it calmly: safe havens like the yen, franc and gold saw no rush of buying. In Europe, the stress point remains France's high borrowing costs.
reads.tot: Oil is back near its recent highs on the risk of attacks reaching Saudi supply. That helps exporters like Canada and hurts big energy importers like Japan and the euro area. Australia and New Zealand also benefit from firm prices for what they sell abroad.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds are betting most heavily against the Canadian dollar, even as a Bank of Canada hike looks likely, which leaves those bets exposed if the loonie keeps rising. They also bet against the kiwi and the euro. In the yen and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.
reads.fiscal: Government finances are weighing on the euro, with France's borrowing costs at their highest in over twenty years before a credit rating review on Friday. In Britain, the October 28 budget comes next and may add help with energy bills.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve is expected to hold rates on October 28 and raise them in December, because high oil is keeping US inflation up. That keeps US rates the highest among the big economies and supports the dollar.
fed.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike very likely.
fed.why: Energy-driven inflation is still too high for the Fed's comfort, and the Gulf conflict is keeping oil near its highs.
fed.watch: Weekly jobless claims on Thursday and whether oil stays high enough to keep the December hike alive; the Fed is in its quiet period until October 28.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada is expected to raise rates on October 28 after governor Tiff Macklem warned that energy will push inflation well above the bank's forecasts. Much of that is already in the Canadian dollar's price.
boc.why: High oil is lifting Canadian inflation, and the bank has said its forecast will be revised sharply higher.
boc.watch: Whether the bank signals more hikes after October, and where oil goes; a hold would be the surprise.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is expected to raise rates on October 28. Inflation cooled slightly in the third quarter but stayed above the bank's target, so the hike case held and supports the kiwi.
rbnz.priced: October 28: hike near certain; a second hike by February fully priced.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the bank's 1–3% target band, and core prices stayed firm even as the headline eased.
rbnz.watch: Whether the bank signals a run of hikes at its October 28 decision, or sounds content after one.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank is expected to hold on October 29 and lean toward a hike in December, as energy keeps euro-area inflation high. That supports the euro, but France's debt worries pull the other way.
ecb.priced: October 29: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Expensive energy is keeping euro-area inflation well above target, even as France's borrowing costs rise.
ecb.watch: What President Christine Lagarde says about December at the October 29 meeting, and Moody's review of France on Friday.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on October 30, but a December hike is increasingly expected. The yen needs that hike, or clear signals of it, to recover from its weakness.
boj.priced: October 30: hold expected; December: hike likely.
boj.why: Inflation is close to the bank's 2% goal and it may raise its inflation forecast this month, which points toward a December move.
boj.watch: Japan's national inflation figures at 6:30 PM CT Thursday, and any hint from governor Kazuo Ueda about timing.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia may raise rates on November 3, with markets now seeing it as close to an even bet. Rising hike odds have lifted the Australian dollar to a three-week high.
rba.priced: November 3: hike close to even odds; December: hike more likely than not.
rba.why: Deputy governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook has worsened, partly because of high oil, and some big banks now expect a November hike.
rba.watch: Australia's third-quarter inflation figures on October 28, the last big input before the November decision.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is all but certain to raise rates on November 5 after UK inflation came in hotter than expected. The pound now moves on whether a second hike follows in December.
boe.priced: November 5: hike near certain; December: second hike a coin toss.
boe.why: Energy is pushing UK inflation far above the 2% target, and the jobs market is still strong.
boe.watch: UK retail sales on Friday and the October 28 budget, which may add help with energy bills.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds rates at zero and a December cut is still possible, because Swiss inflation is near zero. That caps the franc, even though it gains when fear rises.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is barely above zero, and a strong franc keeps import prices low.
snb.watch: The bank's summary of its September policy discussion on Thursday, and any sign it is ready to cut or step into currency markets.

USD.summary: The dollar sits near a three-week low but still has the highest rates among the major currencies, with a Federal Reserve hike expected in December because oil keeps US inflation high.

notes.policy: The Fed is expected to hold in October and hike in December, keeping US rates the highest of the majors.
notes.inflation: High oil keeps US inflation well above the Fed's goal, which supports the case for more hikes.

EUR.summary: The euro is held back by expensive energy and France's rising borrowing costs, even though the European Central Bank leans toward a December hike.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank is expected to hold in October and lean toward a hike in December.
notes.growth: The euro-area economy looks weaker than the US, with France's political strain and high energy costs weighing on it.
notes.inflation: Energy keeps euro-area inflation well above target, which pushes the central bank toward a hike.
notes.tot: Europe imports most of its energy, so high oil and gas prices drain money out of the region.
notes.fiscal: France's borrowing costs are at their highest in over twenty years, ahead of a credit rating review on Friday.

GBP.summary: The pound is near its strongest against the euro in 17 months, because a Bank of England hike in November is all but certain after hot UK inflation.

notes.policy: A Bank of England hike on November 5 is nearly fully priced, with a second in December a coin toss.
notes.growth: UK jobs figures have stayed strong, giving the Bank room to raise rates.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is running far above the 2% target, driven by energy.

JPY.summary: The yen is the weakest major currency on the board, because Japan's rates are far below everyone else's and Japan pays heavily for imported energy.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rates are far below other major banks', though a December hike is increasingly expected.
notes.tot: Japan imports most of its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country and weighs on the yen.

CHF.summary: The franc is held between two forces: it gains when fear rises, but near-zero Swiss inflation keeps the central bank leaning toward a cut.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is near zero, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates and may cut.
notes.risk: The franc is a safe place to park money, so it tends to gain when the Gulf conflict flares.

AUD.summary: The Australian dollar is at a three-week high, as bets on a Reserve Bank of Australia hike in November rise and prices for what Australia sells abroad stay firm.

notes.policy: Markets now see close to even odds of a Reserve Bank of Australia hike on November 3.
notes.growth: Australian jobs fell and unemployment rose to a five-year high, which tempers the case for hikes.
notes.tot: Firm prices for Australia's exports bring money into the country and support the currency.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar is supported by high oil and an expected Bank of Canada hike on October 28, though hedge funds are betting heavily against it.

notes.policy: A Bank of Canada hike on October 28 is close to fully priced.
notes.growth: Canada's housing and shopping figures have been soft, which could limit how far the bank goes after October.
notes.tot: High oil lifts Canada's export income, which supports the currency.

NZD.summary: The kiwi is supported by a Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike next week that markets see as near certain, even after inflation cooled slightly.

notes.policy: A Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on October 28 is close to fully priced, with more expected by February.
notes.growth: New Zealand's factories are having their best stretch since 2021, giving the central bank room to raise rates.
notes.risk: The kiwi tends to fall when investors get nervous, so Gulf fear is a risk for it.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
